$comment: Equity documents: founder IP assignment, vesting agreement, and the Section 83(b) election. These three are the ones most often missing from founder-assembled packages and the most expensive to fix after the fact.

clauses.title: Assignment of Inventions
clauses.benchmark: Present in 88% of IP-critical formation packages
clauses.rationale: Work created before formation belongs to the person who made it unless assigned. This is the single most common diligence defect in early-stage companies.
clauses.body: Each founder hereby irrevocably assigns to the Company all right, title, and interest in every invention, work of authorship, trade secret, know-how, and other intellectual property conceived or reduced to practice in connection with the Company’s business, whether before or after the Effective Date, together with all rights to sue for past infringement.

clauses.title: Work Made For Hire
clauses.rationale: Work-made-for-hire only covers certain categories of work. The backstop assignment is what catches everything else.
clauses.body: All copyrightable works created by a founder within the scope of the Company’s business are [[work made for hire]] under the Copyright Act. To the extent any work does not qualify as a work made for hire, it is assigned to the Company under <<xr:ipa_assign>>.

clauses.title: Prior Inventions
clauses.rationale: A blank prior-inventions schedule is itself a representation. An unlisted prior invention is deemed assigned, which is usually what both sides want.
clauses.body: Each founder shall list on Exhibit A any invention created before the Effective Date that they wish to exclude from <<xr:ipa_assign>>. An unlisted invention is deemed assigned. If a founder lists none, they represent that none exist.

clauses.title: Statutory Invention Carve-Out
clauses.rationale: California requires written notice of the statutory carve-out. An assignment that purports to cover more than the statute allows can be attacked as overbroad.
clauses.body: This assignment does not apply to an invention that the founder developed entirely on their own time without using Company equipment, supplies, facilities, or trade secret information, except for inventions that either relate to the Company’s business or actual or demonstrably anticipated research or development, or result from work performed by the founder for the Company. This notice is given under California Labor Code §2870.

clauses.title: Confidentiality
clauses.rationale: Trade secret protection requires reasonable measures to keep the secret. A written obligation is the cheapest such measure.
clauses.body: Each founder shall hold the Company’s confidential information in confidence during and after their involvement with the Company, and shall not use it except for the Company’s benefit. Nothing in this section prohibits disclosure of a suspected violation of law to a government agency, or disclosure protected by the Defend Trade Secrets Act whistleblower immunity.

clauses.title: No Conflicting Obligations
clauses.benchmark: Present in 79% of IP assignments reviewed in diligence
clauses.rationale: Most founders come from a prior employer with its own invention assignment. This representation is where that conflict surfaces — before an acquirer finds it.
clauses.body: Each founder represents that they are not subject to any agreement with a former employer or other party that conflicts with <<xr:ipa_assign>>, that no Company intellectual property was developed using a former employer’s time, equipment, or confidential information, and that they will not bring any third party’s confidential information onto Company systems.

clauses.title: Open Source Policy
clauses.benchmark: Present in 44% of software company formation packages
clauses.rationale: Copyleft licenses in the wrong part of a codebase can force disclosure of proprietary source. Acquirers scan for this, and remediation late in a deal is expensive.
clauses.body: The Company shall maintain an inventory of open source components incorporated into its products, together with the license governing each. Components under a reciprocal or copyleft license shall not be incorporated into proprietary code without approval recorded under <<xr:@approval>>.

clauses.title: Waiver of Moral Rights
clauses.benchmark: Present in 39% of US IP assignments
clauses.rationale: Moral rights rarely matter in the US, but they do matter if the work is exploited in jurisdictions that recognize them.
clauses.body: To the extent permitted by law, each founder waives all moral rights, rights of attribution, and rights of integrity in the assigned works, and agrees not to assert them against the Company or its licensees or customers.

clauses.title: Further Assurances and Power of Attorney
clauses.rationale: Patent and trademark filings need the inventor's signature. The power of attorney is what lets the Company proceed if a departed founder stops responding.
clauses.body: Each founder shall execute any document and take any action reasonably requested by the Company to perfect, record, or enforce the rights assigned under <<xr:ipa_assign>>, at the Company’s expense. If a founder cannot be reached after reasonable effort, they appoint the Company as their attorney-in-fact for the limited purpose of executing such documents.

clauses.title: Vesting Schedule
clauses.benchmark: Present in 92% of institutionally funded companies
clauses.rationale: Four years with a one-year cliff is the market standard. Deviating costs diligence time without buying anything.
clauses.body: Founder interests vest over {{vestYears}} years measured from {{date}}, with a {{cliff}}-month [[cliff]]. {{cliffPct}} vests on the cliff date; the balance vests in {{monthlyCount}} equal monthly installments. No interest vests after the founder ceases to provide services, except as provided in <<xr:vest_repurchase>>.

clauses.title: Cause and Good Reason
clauses.benchmark: Present in 67% of founder vesting agreements
clauses.rationale: Acceleration and repurchase both turn on these definitions. Leaving them undefined means the most consequential terms in the document are decided in hindsight.
clauses.body: “Cause” means a founder’s conviction of a felony, act of fraud or material dishonesty against the Company, material breach of this agreement not cured within {{cure}} days of written notice, or willful failure to perform assigned duties after written notice. “Good Reason” means a material reduction in duties or compensation, or a relocation of the founder’s principal workplace by more than fifty (50) miles, in each case without the founder’s consent and after {{cure}} days to cure.

clauses.title: Leave of Absence
clauses.rationale: Silence means vesting continues through an indefinite leave. Tolling is standard, but it interacts with protected leave and should not be applied automatically.
clauses.body: Vesting continues during any leave of absence protected by law. For any other leave exceeding {{cure}} days, vesting is tolled for the period beyond {{cure}} days and the vesting dates are extended accordingly.

clauses.title: Repurchase Right
clauses.rationale: Vesting without a repurchase right is decorative. The repurchase is the mechanism that actually recovers unvested equity.
clauses.body: If a founder ceases to provide services for any reason, the Company may repurchase all unvested interests at the lower of original cost or fair market value, exercisable for ninety (90) days following cessation. The repurchase price may be paid in cash or by cancellation of indebtedness.

clauses.title: Double-Trigger Acceleration
clauses.benchmark: Present in 74% of venture-track founder vesting agreements
clauses.rationale: Single-trigger acceleration depresses the purchase price because the acquirer loses retention. Double-trigger is the compromise both sides accept.
clauses.body: If the Company is acquired and a founder is terminated without Cause or resigns for Good Reason within twelve (12) months following the closing, all unvested interests vest immediately. Cause and Good Reason have the meanings given in <<xr:vest_definitions>>.

clauses.title: Restriction on Transfer of Unvested Interests
clauses.rationale: Transferring unvested equity would defeat the repurchase right by putting it beyond the Company's reach.
clauses.body: Unvested interests may not be transferred, pledged, or encumbered. Any attempted transfer is void, and the Company’s repurchase right under <<xr:vest_repurchase>> continues to apply to any interest transferred in violation of this section.

clauses.title: Section 83(b) Election
clauses.rationale: Without the election, the founder recognizes ordinary income as each tranche vests, measured at the then-current value. With it, they recognize almost nothing now.
clauses.body: The undersigned hereby makes an election under Section 83(b) of the Internal Revenue Code with respect to {{shareCount}} shares of {{company}} acquired on {{date}} for {{parValue}} per share, subject to the vesting described in <<xr:vest_schedule>>. The undersigned includes in gross income for the current taxable year the excess of the fair market value of the shares over the amount paid, which the undersigned determines to be zero.

clauses.title: Filing Instructions
clauses.rationale: The election is lost by late filing far more often than by any substantive error. The deadline runs from the grant date, not from the tax year.
clauses.body: This election must be postmarked to the IRS office where the undersigned files their federal return within thirty (30) days of {{date}} — that is {{d83bDeadline}}. Send it by certified mail with return receipt and retain the receipt. Provide a copy to the Company for its records. There is no procedure to cure a late filing.

clauses.title: Spousal Signature
clauses.rationale: In a community property state the spouse may hold an interest in the shares, and the election is cleaner if they sign it too.
clauses.body: If the undersigned is married and resides in a community property jurisdiction, the undersigned’s spouse should also sign this election with respect to any community property interest in the shares.
